prompt: Which protocol distributed text-based discussion across newsgroups before the web?
explanation: Usenet, launched in 1980 at Duke and the University of North Carolina, distributed text-based discussion across thousands of named newsgroups using the Network News Transfer Protocol. It built much of the cultural grammar — FAQ documents, threads, flame wars, moderators — that the web later inherited.

prompt: The graphical web browser whose 1993 release brought the web to ordinary users was:
explanation: NCSA Mosaic (1993), developed by Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina at the University of Illinois, was the first widely-used graphical web browser. Andreessen later co-founded Netscape (1994), whose Navigator browser dominated the late 1990s before Internet Explorer's rise.

prompt: The collaborative encyclopedia launched in January 2001 by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger is _________.
explanation: Wikipedia, launched January 2001, demonstrated large-scale collaborative knowledge production using Ward Cunningham's wiki format. By 2010 the English Wikipedia had over 3 million articles; today it remains one of the most successful single instances of the open-web ethos.

prompt: What was the dominant business model of Web 1.0?
options: The portal — Yahoo!, MSN, AOL.com competing to be users' default home page
correctAnswer: The portal — Yahoo!, MSN, AOL.com competing to be users' default home page
explanation: The Web 1.0 era was dominated by portals: Yahoo!, MSN, AOL.com, Excite, and others competed to be users' default home page, monetising attention through banner advertising and directory listings. Search was a feature within portals, not a destination. The model was almost entirely displaced within a decade by search and social.

prompt: Match each early-web tool to its purpose:

pairs.right: Low-cost personal-publishing tool acquired by Google in 2003
Open-source publishing platform that became the dominant CMS
Collaborative encyclopedia using the wiki format

explanation: These tools made web publishing accessible to non-technical users, breaking the early-web requirement that authors handle their own HTML and hosting. The blog and wiki formats they enabled were the foundations of the citizen-publishing layer that has continued to develop into the modern creator economy.

prompt: Facebook's launch of the algorithmic News Feed in 2006:
options: Introduced an algorithmically curated stream of friends' activity that became the template for nearly every subsequent social platform
Removed all advertising from the platform
correctAnswer: Introduced an algorithmically curated stream of friends' activity that became the template for nearly every subsequent social platform
explanation: The 2006 News Feed introduced the now-ubiquitous algorithmically curated stream of friends' activity. Combined with the real-name social graph that distinguished Facebook from earlier networks (Friendster, MySpace), it produced a system much more legible to advertisers and to algorithmic ranking. The pattern has been imitated across every major social platform since.

prompt: How much did Elon Musk pay to acquire Twitter in October 2022?
explanation: Musk's $44 billion acquisition closed in October 2022 after a contentious legal process. The platform was rebranded as X in 2023 and underwent deep cost-cutting, mass content-moderation changes, advertiser exodus, and substantial declines in active users.

prompt: TikTok is owned by the Chinese company _________.
explanation: ByteDance owns TikTok and its Chinese counterpart Douyin. The Chinese ownership and the resulting US national-security debate (multiple proposed bans, the 2024 divestment law, the Supreme Court hearing) is one of the central technology-policy questions of the period.

prompt: What did Snapchat pioneer that has since been widely copied?
options: Ephemeral messaging that auto-deletes after viewing, and the Stories format
correctAnswer: Ephemeral messaging that auto-deletes after viewing, and the Stories format
explanation: Snapchat (2011) pioneered ephemeral messaging — messages deleted after viewing — and the Stories format that has been copied to Instagram (2016), Facebook, WhatsApp, YouTube, LinkedIn, Twitter, and many others. The format's spread illustrates how rapidly successful interaction patterns are absorbed across platforms.

prompt: Match each platform to a defining innovation or distinguishing feature:

pairs.right: Real-name social graph and algorithmically ranked News Feed
Directional follow graph; one-to-many real-time public discussion
For You Page recommending across the whole catalogue, not just followed accounts

explanation: These three platforms illustrate the evolution of social networking. Facebook used a bilateral real-name graph; Twitter introduced a directional graph optimised for one-to-many broadcasting; TikTok abandoned the social graph as the primary signal in favour of recommendation across the whole catalogue. Each shift produced different content patterns and different commercial economics.

prompt: What was Facebook's first widely-known feed-ranking algorithm called?
explanation: EdgeRank, introduced by Facebook around 2010, scored News Feed posts by an affinity-weight-time-decay formula. Its successors evolved into the deep-learning ranking systems used today, but EdgeRank was the first widely-known instance of platform feed-ranking moving away from chronological order.

prompt: Vosoughi, Roy, and Aral's 2018 MIT Media Lab study found that:
options: False news travels slower than true news on Twitter
False news travels faster and farther than true news on Twitter, in part because of surprise and emotional salience
Algorithms have no measurable effect on virality
Twitter has no false news problem
correctAnswer: False news travels faster and farther than true news on Twitter, in part because of surprise and emotional salience
explanation: The Vosoughi-Roy-Aral study (Science, 2018) found that false news on Twitter travelled significantly faster and reached more people than true news. The mechanism was not ideological bias but engagement bias: surprise and emotional salience predicted sharing, and false news scored highly on both. Subsequent work has documented similar patterns on other platforms.

prompt: TikTok's recommendation feed, launched with the international product in 2018, is called the For You _________.
explanation: The For You Page (FYP) recommends across the whole catalogue of recent uploads, using strong signals from very short watch sessions to converge on a personalised feed within minutes. The combination of vertical video, immediate behavioural learning, and full-catalogue recommendation made TikTok the most engagement-optimised mass medium yet built.

prompt: What is the typical structure of a modern recommender system?
options: A single deep neural network scoring every item in the catalogue
Two stages — candidate generation via cheap embedding similarity, then ranking via expensive ML models
A keyword filter applied to chronological feeds
Random selection from a quality whitelist
correctAnswer: Two stages — candidate generation via cheap embedding similarity, then ranking via expensive ML models
explanation: Modern recommenders are typically two-stage: candidate generation retrieves a few hundred candidates from the full catalogue using cheap embedding-similarity methods, and ranking applies a more expensive model to score candidates against engagement-prediction targets. The targets typically combine click-through, watch-time, follow, comment, share, and downstream signals into a weighted multi-objective.

prompt: Match each algorithm-related concept to its description:

pairs.right: Hypothesis that personalisation isolates users in ideological echo chambers; held up worse than expected empirically
Combining click-through, watch-time, share, comment, and other signals into a weighted target
EU obligation for very large platforms to offer non-personalised feed options

explanation: Each of these has shaped the algorithmic-feed debate. The filter bubble was the dominant early concern but the empirical case is weaker than the original hypothesis. Multi-objective optimisation is how the systems actually work. The DSA's non-personalised-feed obligation is one of the first concrete regulatory constraints on platform feed design, requiring transparency and user choice that platforms previously avoided.

prompt: Which year did YouTube launch its Partner Program for creator revenue sharing?
explanation: The YouTube Partner Program (2007) introduced revenue-sharing on advertising, with creators receiving roughly 55% of ad revenue from videos on their channels. It was the first platform-scale monetisation program enabling individuals to earn substantial income from creator activity.

prompt: Which YouTuber reached over 300 million subscribers, the largest individual subscriber base on the platform?
explanation: MrBeast (Jimmy Donaldson) crossed 300 million YouTube subscribers in 2024, becoming the most-subscribed individual channel on the platform. The scale is comparable to or exceeds the global audience of major broadcast networks.

prompt: The newsletter platform that has allowed many writers to assemble subscription-funded independent practices is _________.
explanation: Substack (2017) combined an email newsletter platform with subscription-payment infrastructure. Bari Weiss, Andrew Sullivan, Glenn Greenwald, Matt Taibbi, and many others assembled six-figure subscription revenues that allowed them to leave traditional media jobs.

prompt: The largest single revenue stream for top creators is typically:
explanation: While platform ad-revenue share provides a baseline ($1–5 CPM is typical), brand sponsorships — paid product mentions, dedicated videos, integrated promotions — typically generate the largest share of income for top creators, often dwarfing platform revenue. Affiliate marketing provides a third significant stream.

prompt: Match each creator-economy infrastructure to its function:

pairs.right: Direct subscriber-payment platform independent of ad revenue
Live-streaming platform with subscription, bits, and direct-payment monetisation
Match brands with creators, handle disclosure, payment, and performance tracking

explanation: These three platforms span the creator-economy infrastructure stack. Patreon provides direct-payment alternatives to platform ad-revenue; Twitch built monetisation tailored to live-streaming; influencer-marketing platforms formalised the brand-deal market that produces the largest revenue stream for most professional creators.

prompt: Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act provides that:
options: Platforms must moderate all illegal content within 24 hours
Platforms are not treated as publishers of user-generated content and have immunity for good-faith moderation
All online speech is protected without limit
correctAnswer: Platforms are not treated as publishers of user-generated content and have immunity for good-faith moderation
explanation: Section 230(c)(1) provides that platforms are not treated as the publisher or speaker of user-generated content. Section 230(c)(2) provides immunity for good-faith decisions to remove or restrict objectionable content. Without Section 230, modern platforms hosting user-generated content at scale would not be economically viable.

prompt: The EU's 2024 platform regulatory framework is the:
explanation: The Digital Services Act, applying to very large platforms from 2023 and fully from 2024, imposes obligations including transparency reporting, user-facing reasons for content removal, systemic-risk assessments, researcher data access, non-personalised feed options, and prohibition of certain dark-pattern designs. Penalties can reach 6% of global revenue.

prompt: Meta's quasi-judicial body that reviews high-profile content decisions is the _________ Board.
explanation: Meta's Oversight Board, founded 2020, reviews high-profile content decisions and publishes binding case decisions. The Board is funded through a long-term trust to insulate it from Meta operational pressure, though critics question whether the structure achieves genuine independence.

prompt: Why is content moderation at scale fundamentally hard?
options: Any consistent rule produces unacceptable edge cases at platform scale, while inconsistent rules produce accusations of bias
correctAnswer: Any consistent rule produces unacceptable edge cases at platform scale, while inconsistent rules produce accusations of bias
explanation: Sarah T. Roberts, Tarleton Gillespie, and other moderation scholars have made this point repeatedly: at the scale of billions of posts daily, any rule produces large numbers of edge cases that create reputational and legal harm; making exceptions for hard cases produces accusations of bias. The honest assessment is that moderation at scale is a fundamentally hard problem with only trade-offs between different kinds of failure.

prompt: Match each platform-governance instrument to its jurisdiction:

pairs.right: US — platform liability immunity for user-generated content
EU — systemic-risk obligations on very large platforms
UK — duty of care toward UK users with focus on illegal content

explanation: These three instruments illustrate the regulatory variety platforms now navigate. Section 230 is permissive (immunity); the DSA is procedural (transparency and risk-assessment obligations); the Online Safety Act is substantive (duty-of-care framework). Major platforms increasingly operate jurisdictional moderation regimes that vary by user country.

prompt: What term originally described face-swap videos using generative adversarial networks?
explanation: The term 'deepfakes' came from a 2017 Reddit account that used GAN-based face-swap techniques primarily for non-consensual pornography. The original use produced platform bans and the first legislative responses; the underlying technology has since been substantially superseded by foundation-model video generation.

prompt: ChatGPT's launch in November 2022 reached 100 million users in approximately:
options: Two months — the fastest consumer-product growth in history at that point
correctAnswer: Two months — the fastest consumer-product growth in history at that point
explanation: ChatGPT reached 100 million users within two months of launch, the fastest consumer-product adoption in history at that point. The combination of accessible chat interface and capable underlying model brought generative AI from a research curiosity to mass-market software within weeks.

prompt: The cross-industry standard for cryptographic content provenance attaches signed metadata to authentic media; the abbreviation is _________.
explanation: The C2PA (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity) Content Credentials specification, supported by Adobe, Microsoft, OpenAI, and others, attaches signed metadata to media to enable verification of capture vs generation. Adoption is voluntary and limited; the technology is one component of a still-incomplete defensive infrastructure.

prompt: What is the 'information-stack problem' caused by widespread AI generation?
options: AI is too expensive to deploy
The internet's ecosystem assumed plausible content required human effort; AI generation invalidated that assumption, polluting search, social, and verification infrastructure
correctAnswer: The internet's ecosystem assumed plausible content required human effort; AI generation invalidated that assumption, polluting search, social, and verification infrastructure
explanation: Search engines, social platforms, recommender systems, and consumers' bullshit-detectors were calibrated against a cost structure where producing plausible text, images, audio, and video required substantial human effort. Generative AI invalidated that assumption. Pink Slime AI news sites, AI-voiced robocalls, AI-image political content, and SEO 'slop' have demonstrated the consequences.

prompt: Match each AI-era response to its purpose:

pairs.right: First comprehensive AI regulation requiring labelling of generated content and risk assessment
Embedded signals in generated text/images for post-hoc detection by the model provider
Verification that an online presence corresponds to a unique human (Worldcoin, EU Digital Identity)

explanation: These three responses span regulatory, technical, and identity-verification approaches to the AI-media problem. None has demonstrated comprehensive effectiveness; the honest assessment is that we are in a transitional period when the institutions, norms, and infrastructure required for AI-saturated information environments have not yet been built.
